prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Operating and Financial Metrics (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 17px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Metric" · longest unbreakable word 92px · one-line width 452px
  col 2: header "FY 2022" · longest unbreakable word 67px · one-line width 67px
  col 3: header "FY 2023" · longest unbreakable word 69px · one-line width 69px
  col 4: header "FY 2024" · longest unbreakable word 64px · one-line width 68px
  col 5: header "Q1 2025" · longest unbreakable word 70px · one-line width 70px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 557px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 556px.
Fixed: content, font, 17px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 557px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Track six operating and financial metrics across FY 2022–FY 2024 and Q1 2025 so readers can assess trends and current performance.","reading":"Readers identify the metric in the row header, then scan the four period columns left to right. Comparison happens horizontally within each row and vertically across metrics, so both row-label readability and period alignment matter.","groups":["FY 2022, FY 2023 and FY 2024 form a historical annual series and should share a consistent width and rhythm.","Q1 2025 is the latest/current period; it belongs with the other periods but can be treated as a distinct endpoint.","The Metric column has a separate row-label role and needs enough width to keep labels scannable."],"keep_intact":["All numeric values and units: 112%, 71.3%, 38.2%, $1,840, $318.4M, $41.2M.","Period headers FY 2022, FY 2023, FY 2024 and Q1 2025 on one line where possible.","No breaking of currency amounts, percentages or identifiers."],"may_wrap":["Long Metric labels at word boundaries, especially 'Sales and marketing expense as a percentage of revenue', 'Net revenue retention, trailing twelve months', 'Customer acquisition cost, blended', 'Annual recurring revenue, end of period' and 'Free cash flow, trailing twelve months'."]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[202,88,90,85,91],"idea":"Maximize the row-label column while holding each period column at the minimum width that keeps its header and values intact."},{"name":"B","widths":[180,94,94,94,94],"idea":"Balance label readability with an even, rhythmic set of four equal period columns for easy horizontal comparison."},{"name":"C","widths":[156,100,100,100,100],"idea":"Prioritize generous period columns and comparison rhythm, accepting more wrapping in the metric labels."}]}
